items.title: New from Chicago: A full-color visual history of how we connected the world
items.author: 557489585.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
items.content:
A beautifully illustrated, first-of-its-kind chronicle of road maps through the ages.

Road maps are the most common form of map that most of us regularly interact with while we all seek to find our way from here to there. Today, the digital maps on our devices are just the latest in a series of cartographic innovations designed to make transportation of people and goods easier and more predictable. Whether traveling on foot, in a vehicle, or by animal, people have long created and relied on roads, and efforts to map these overland routes predate the invention of the printing press. Yet the vast majority of road maps have been produced only within the last five hundred years—and even more specifically within the last century.

Historian Jeremy Black is the first to chart the tale of road maps, beginning with the “Peutinger Map,” which illustrated the roads famously connecting the Roman Empire. From the time of antiquity, Black guides the reader through the centuries all the way to the modern age, when the invention of the automobile spurred the creation of roads and road maps like nothing before. Over the course of this journey, Black illuminates the integral role maps played in the development of government infrastructures through time and across all the inhabited continents. And, arriving in the present day, Black shows how technology may soon make the paper road map obsolete even as it builds on the conventions of the preceding centuries.

Featuring a series of full-color maps from the British Library’s collection and beyond,

is an eye-opening visual story of how modern civilizations traversed, constructed, and connected their worlds.

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Bad surprises are bad
items.author: bounces+p9ugg2oe7li9hdkx6n2aqhpp0kw46trhklpz@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about avoiding bad surprises. Good leadership is often about : You have to decide when to share bad news and when to handle it yourself. But you should always strive to avoid sitting on bad news so long that it becomes a bad surprise for your team.

If you see bad news coming, don’t sit on it and hope things change for the better. Make sure you communicate that bad news early so the team can either prevent it or plan for it.

It can be very easy to think you might save the situation before it gets bad, or that maybe things won’t turn out as bad as you expect. Hope is not a strategy. The longer you wait, the worse the surprise.

How much you share will depend on whether you’re sharing up, sharing with co-leaders, or sharing with the team you’re leading. When sharing up and with co-leaders, share more and share faster. When sharing with the team you’re leading, share more selectively, but do not allow your team to be blindsided by bad news.

You should also strive to share bad news along with some sort of plan or at least a suggestion to prevent or mitigate it. It’s much easier to receive bad news if it’s paired with a plan of action.

items.title: It's Royals Hall of Fame time
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
If you’re a nerd for baseball like most of us, team-specific Halls of Fame are generally a good time. It’s an ode to players who, in some way, made a positive impact to the franchise. They may not sniff the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown, but they mean something to a team and its fanbase.

Now that we are just over 10 years removed from the improbable and massive championship seasons of 2014 and 2015, it's not a surprise that this Royals Hall of Fame ballot for this cycle is capital “S” stacked. Actually, it’s all caps STACKED. Twelve players are up for election and I can make a convincing case to varying degrees for 11 of them.

The fan vote opened on Monday. I am going to present the candidates in order of my opinion of worthiness on this ballot. A stacked ballot like this requires some strategy, so guys in their final year of eligibility get a bit of a longer look and there will maybe be a surprise or two down at the bottom.

The fan voting is just one cog in the Royals Hall of Fame machine. From the press release about how votes are tabulated:

Fans will be joined by other voters, including all living members of the Royals Hall of Fame, the Royals Ownership Group, members of the Royals Hall of Fame Executive Board, select members of the Kansas City Chapter of the Baseball Writers Association of America and Kansas City media, and current Royals front office staff with at least 15 years of service, in selecting any Royals Hall of Fame inductees. The online fan ballot will account for 12 full votes for each of the top five vote getters. Any candidate receiving 75% of the vote will be elected and scheduled for induction during the 2027 Royals season. Eligible alumni that receive at least 10% of the vote can remain on the ballot for five regular phase election cycles.

It’s not the most transparent of systems because who knows how many votes are cast. Or how many players an individual can vote for. The only thing we know is that if a player finishes in the top five of the fan ballot, they get 12 votes. That’s probably enough of a push that a player who doesn’t finish in the top five will fail to get the required 75%.

I find it hilarious that Beltrán is the Hall of Fame in Cooperstown yet is on the outside looking in when it comes to the Royals Hall. Beltrán spent parts of seven of his 20 major league seasons in KC, winning the Rookie of the Year award in 1999, hitting .287/.352/.483 while accumulating 24.8 bWAR. His prime was spent in New York with the Mets and he went into the Baseball Hall of Fame with a Mets cap, but his tenure in Kansas City was exceptionally good.

Yes, context matters. In the instance of Beltrán, he played on some of the worst teams in franchise history, feuded with the front office over an injury and couldn’t wait to get out of town so he could play for a winning team. When he was finally dealt away, the Royals landed catcher John Buck, third baseman Mark Teahen and pitcher Mike Wood. Not great! Also, not Beltrán’s fault.

Beltrán is ninth all-time on the Royals in position player bWAR, fifth in OPS (just behind Bobby Witt Jr. at .835) and first all-time in stolen base percentage with an 87.7 percent success rate. The counting stats aren’t there because Beltrán played in only 795 games for the Royals, 23rd all-time, but he was the best player by a mile on those bad Royals teams. Perhaps he’s been overshadowed by the beloved players from the Royals World Championship run a decade after he departed, but it’s absurd that he hasn’t gotten in.

If you believe in that first-ballot Hall of Famer kind of lore, Greinke is in. Besides, it would look kind of silly to go through this exercise and not have Greinke enshrined at the end of it.

Greinke debuted in 2004 and finished his Royals career in 2023 after stops in Milwaukee, Anaheim, Los Angeles, Arizona and Houston. He ranks seventh in franchise history in innings pitched (1,387.1), fourth in strikeouts (1,101) and sixth in fWAR (26.8). His 2009 season was one the best in franchise history where he posted a 2.16 ERA, 242 strikeouts and a career-best 8.7 fWAR, culminating in the AL Cy Young Award.

He was traded to the Brewers after the 2010 season for two players also up for induction.

You should vote for Greinke just so you can hear his acceptance speech.

I’m not sure how LoCain didn’t make it into the Royals Hall his first time on the ballot. He was the best player on the Royals World Championship team in 2015 and their second-best behind 2025 Royals Hall of Fame inductee Alex Gordon on the 2014 pennant winners. That fact alone gets you the rubber stamp treatment as far as I’m concerned.

I feel like I’m bringing myself to the edge of insanity when it comes to Cain. When you gather all the stats from the five years from 2013 to 2017, Cain was the best player on the Royals and it’s not even close. How he wasn’t elected the first time he was eligible doesn’t compute.

He could do everything. Most of all…”HE CAN FLY!”

Like Beltrán, this is Butler’s final year on the Royals Hall ballot. Unlike Beltrán, Butler is not going to be elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame.

If you’re one of those who needs a complete ballplayer to be in these Halls of Fame, you’re not going to be a fan of Butler. He was drafted as a third baseman. That seemed to last about a week. He moved across the diamond to first and wasn’t much better. His defensive destiny was to forget the glove all together. Hitting was Butler’s game.

It feels fairly obvious to me that Butler is one of the top hitters in franchise history. He’s fourth all-time in batting average (.295), ninth in hits (1,273), ninth in total bases (1,938), eighth in doubles (276) and eighth in RBI (628). He’s just outside the franchise top 10 in OBP (.356, good for 13th), slugging (.449, 15th) and OPS (.808, 12th). His best season was in 2012 when he hit .313/.373/.510 with 29 home runs and 107 RBI, won a Silver Slugger and was selected to the All-Star team. He should’ve been a participant in the Home Run Derby, damnit. Boooooooo!

5-6-7 - Kelvin Herrera/Wade Davis/Greg Holland

I understand Hall of Fame voting on any level is serious business. Serious Business! Sometimes, you just have to do something that veers from the norm. I defer to my pal Mike Engel for how this should work.

How perfect would that be? So perfect that it needs to happen.

If I mention "HDH", you know what I'm talking about. Maybe you think that only two of the three listed above are Royals Hall-worthy. If that’s the case, I humbly request you check yourself. You’re telling me you would vote to induct Snap and Pop and ignore Crackle? Athos and Aramis are in, but Porthos is out? Do you make a sandwich with bacon and lettuce and no tomato? Get all the way outta here with that.

The Royals trio redefined how bullpens were used in the postseason and, then, revolutionized the art in the regular season. Herrera could’ve closed for 29 teams but accepted his seventh inning role. Davis closed out the World Series in 2015, but his performance on either side of a rain delay in Game Six of the ALCS is the stuff of legend. And all Holland did was sacrifice his UCL for the club while dominating hitters in the ninth. If any one of those guys isn’t a stud, I’m not sure there’s a flag flying for 2014 or 2015.

Be bold. Put them in as a trio. (I thought about listing them as 7/8/9, but that would be too low. Appropriate, but low.)

Soria is in a bit of a difficult position when it comes to franchise history. Acquired as a Rule 5 draft selection ahead of the 2007 season, he departed as a free agent after 2012. He then rejoined the club for the 2016 season. Bad timing, no?

His closer bonafides are undisputed. He's third in club history with 162 saves, trailing only Quis and Monty. So he's in this weird reliever tier where he's not in the upper echelon of Royals closers, nor is he in the triumvirate of postseason relievers. Still, I think he's deserving of a spot in the Royals Hall. It may take some time to get there.

This is where things could get contentious. Hosmer was a good player in Royals history and a pivotal player in the championship run. More than anyone, he seemed to be the guy in the middle of just about every pivotal moment in the Royals championship run. From the triple in the bottom of the 12th in the 2014 Wild Card game to the mad dash home in the ninth inning of Game Five of the 2015 World Series, Hoz was The Man.

He gets in, but not this year.

Mooooooose. Moustakas was another key guy on those championship teams, but lacks the numbers and moments of his teammates. He does rank ninth on the all-time franchise list for home runs (139). A two-time All-Star with the Royals, he briefly held the franchise record for most home runs in a season when he clubbed 38 in 2017.

Somehow, it just worked. Escobar was the catalyst of those championship teams, leading off (despite a sub .300 OBP) and doing things like the Esky Ambush to, you know, hit leadoff inside the park home runs in the first game of the World Series. His best season was probably in 2012, but he filled up his trophy case in 2015, winning the Gold Glove, starting the All-Star game and picking up the ALCS MVP Award.

He's 10th all-time on the franchise hit list with 1,208 and ninth in steals with 160.

Sorry. Somebody has to be last. And when you're on a list of true franchise legends with World Series rings and Baseball Hall of Fame credentials, you kind of get pushed to the bottom. He was their big free agent signing in 2016 from San Diego. He was good in the rotation for the Royals that year, but later scuffled and finished his time as a solid closer for the club.

items.title: The Sunday Ramble - Free Agent Edition
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
The mad dash that figures to be baseball's truncated offseason begins in earnest on Monday at 4 p.m. as that is the hour when all free agents will be eligible to negotiate with other teams. It seems like a perfect time to dust off the Ramble and rank the top 20 free agents. While the Royals, as usual, won't make a play for the top tier of free agents, this year's class is incredibly thin. In other words, it's Tarik Skubal at the top and then there's everyone else. That means the Royals could be—should be—in the hunt for several free agents that are on the list below.

There are a handful of solid, and realistic, options on this list for the Royals. Later this week, I'll take a look at players outside my list of the top 20 that the Royals should be considering.

We start, like every other free agent list you will see, with the undisputed heavyweight of the 2026-27 Free Agent Class. It looked like his walk year was going to be sunk when he hit the IL with elbow issues early in the season, but he dodged Tommy John surgery and opted for a NanoScope procedure. He made it back to the mound a month later and proved he was still The Man when it came to starting pitchers.

The sky is the limit for the contact he will land. Left-handed, 30-years-old and the clear marquee player in an overall weak free agent class, the bidding will be fierce. I would imagine he'll go off the board as we close in on December 1.

King missed considerable time in 2025 with a shoulder injury and a knee issue. He signed a three-year deal in San Diego with a couple of opt outs, which is why he’s here…King decided to take a $5 million buyout and passed up $28 million in 2027 and $30 million that would’ve been due to him in 2028. That’s a chunk of change he’s expecting to recoup on the market, obviously plus some extra. He features five pitches with some insane movement on his sweeper and change that make him difficult to barrel. A Statcast darling to be sure, which means he’s going to continue to get paid.

He will be 32 in May and the number of starting pitchers that old who have received a four-year deal can be counted on one hand.

Yeah, I have Rogers this high for a few reasons. He’s one of the younger starting pitching options on the market (he will be 29 next year) and he’s a strike-thrower. A rough start to his 2026 season skewed his numbers, but he rebounded to post up the best walk rate of his career and a 3.45 FIP against a 4.03 ERA. In other words, the back of the baseball card numbers may put off some people, but the metrics insist this guy is a quality arm. Put him on a team with a forward-looking pitching lab and watch him take off.

He’s a guy the Royals should most definitely be checking on, but the competition for his services is likely to drive the price out of their comfort zone.

Sato won the NPB Triple Crown, the first player to do it since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. You’ll remember the reluctance from MLB teams to pursue Murakami as there was some question how his contact skills would play in the majors. It turns out they were just fine. There’s a little more risk here in that Sato is an even more aggressive hitter, and there are questions about where he will play defensively, but he should do better than Murakami’s two-year deal with the White Sox.

A corner infielder isn’t a fit, but I’m waiting for the days the Royals step up and play in this market.

5 and 6) Randy Arozarena - LF & Seiya Suzuki - RF

Full disclosure: I adore Randy Arozarena. The guy is a blast and, in his walk year, had the best offensive season of his career. He should get paid, but I don’t like the idea of handing out a long-term contract to a 32-year-old corner outfielder who is a defensive liability. While there’s an allure to right-handed pop, there should be an aversion to a long-term deal he will most certainly be seeking.

The Royals desperately need help in left, but defensive limitations and what is certain to be a lofty price tag means Arozarena isn’t the guy here.

Suzuki sure feels like Arozarena’s corner outfield free agent counterpart. You could probably put these guys in same slot when ranking free agents. (Which I sort of did!) Suzuki features more patience at the plate and better defense. In doing research for this edition of the newsletter I learned that Suzuki is one of four hitters to post an OPS+ of 125 or higher in each of the last four seasons. Not even Bobby Witt Jr. can make that claim. Impressive.

Like Arozarena, he's 32 next year and there are some Statcast warnings that started bubbling up last summer, like a decline in exit velocity and barrel rate that ended up being the lowest of his major league career. Corner outfielders over 30 are scary.

Given my admitted bias against relief pitchers, perhaps I have lost my mind for putting a setup guy this high on the list. Except when you’re bullpen mates with Mason Miller, you’re always going to be the eighth inning guy. Morejón is close to Miller on the filth-factor, tickling triple-digits and missing bats with regularlity. Plus, he’s just 28 years old. The top reliever on the market. Oh! There's also the possibility that a team could move him to the rotation. A four-pitch mix (four-seam, sinker, change and slider) makes him an option. Besides, if it doesn't work, the bullpen thing seems to be just fine.

I generally think paying a reliever big bucks in free agency is folly, but if Morejón is looking at a four year deal, I’d be all over that. The Royals need velocity and swing and miss in their bullpen and the lefty would most definitely bring that.

Other pitchers got the headlines this October, but I enjoyed the fact that Peralta was throwing meaningful innings in the World Series. You know the story: Traded by the Brewers to the Mets, he had a horrible first few months of the season. As in a 4.99 ERA and 4.45 FIP. Everything the Mets touch…yadda, yadda, yadda. Jettisoned to the Rays at the trade deadline, Peralta, under the tutelage of pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the other smart people in the organization, raised his arm angle, got more extension and drive in his delivery and worked exclusively from the stretch. He pitched to a 3.25 ERA and 3.93 FIP down the stretch. Are the changes sticky? It’s gonna cost a team to find out.

That strong last couple of months, plus a solid World Series means his stock is on the ascent. He doesn’t pitch deep in games so you’d want a solid bullpen in place behind him. Until further notice, that eliminates the Royals.

Lowe, who will be 32 next year, had the best all-around season of his career for the Pirates in 2026. Good timing. He’s always been an above-average bat with 30-home run pop while manning the keystone. The Pirates transformed his glovework and he became an elite defender up the middle last summer. It will probably take a three-year deal to rope him in and he will presumably be attached to a qualifying offer to boot.

Second base is an interesting position in this class, something that is rarely said. Are the Royals set with Michael Massey? Both are Gold Glove finalists, if you’re into that sort of thing.

A bat-first catcher with solid plate discipline will always get some free agent looks, as a savvy club will work to improve his framing. Not sure his pop times can improve, though. Jeffers missed time with a broken hamate bone and really ran out of steam at the end of the year.

I expect the Twins to drop a qualifying offer here. That could be too tempting to pass.

If you’re looking for a Proven Closer™ in this free agent class, Bednar is your guy. He’s racked up 146 saves over his career split between Pittsburgh and the Yankees. Apart from a weird season where he struggled with his command and the runs allowed in 2024 and missed time with an oblique injury, he’s been good for around 30 saves, a 2.25 ERA and 2.0 fWAR. He doesn’t have that closer flash but gets the job done.

12) Jazz Chisholm Jr. - 2B

A polarizing player to say the least, Chisholm has averaged nearly 4 fWAR over the last three seasons. He does it through a combination of decent offensive production, solid defense and some good baserunning. Yeah, he said he was going to go 50-50 in 2026, but he does have one 30/30 season under his belt. The power will take a dip when he leaves New Yankee Stadium, but he’s a solid everyday player who could fill out a lineup for a contender.

A newly-minted World Champion, Bauers is an interesting case. For the first five years of his big league career, he was a below average hitter and defender. Just a guy. In 2025, he added on base percentage to his toolkit and became an above-average hitter for the first time in his career. This year, he unlocked power. The result? A career best offensive season where he hit .266/.389/.484, good for a 143 wRC+. Let’s say he’s peaking at the absolute best time. There’s some risk there, especially given that his future home lies as a designated hitter.

How is it possible that Sonny Gray has pitched in 14 big league seasons? His strikeout rate tumbled in ’26, but he still managed to put up a 2.72 ERA, a 3.47 FIP and a 3.4 fWAR. Dip in punchouts aside, he’s been crazy consistent the last three seasons. He’s a workhorse, too, averaging 175 innings over the last four years. He declined his side of a $30 million mutual option to hit the open market.

I’d be nervous at giving him a second year, but he’s a perfect short-term rotation piece for any team looking for innings from their rotation. In other words, he’s attractive to every single team in the majors.

Holmes saw his season go sideways when he took a comebacker off his leg, which broke his fibula. He missed three months. When healthy, he’s a ground ball specialist two years removed from the bullpen. The bullpen to rotation jump in his mid thirties reminds me of Seth Lugo. Holmes could be an attractive option to pick up some innings and keep the ball on the ground at the back of a rotation, including the Royals.

Happ has been a solid 3.0 fWAR kind of guy throughout his career, but experienced the roughest offensive season of his career in 2026, hitting .218/.326/.412 and a 107 wRC+. Bad timing for Happ but perhaps an opportunity for a club looking for a solid option in left. There’s been rumors of interest in Happ on the part of the Royals for the last couple of seasons. Expect those rumors to pick up steam over the next 30 days. He would certainly be an upgrade as a bounceback candidate.

Another polarizing second baseman, but for a different reason. If this was 1977, a career .330 batting average would have you near the top of this list. Too bad for Arraez, we are heading into 2027. To his credit, he worked with Ron Washington for half a season in San Francisco and completely remade himself as a defender. He would be lower on this ranking but not for Wash. This will be his sixth different team since 2024.

Shoulder problems and a Tommy John surgery limited Mahle to eight starts between 2023 and 2024. The shoulder barked again in 2025. That meant his first foray into free agency wasn’t as lucrative as he probably had hoped as he signed a one-year $10 million deal with the Giants. Like everyone in San Francisco, he underwhelmed, posting a 5.13 ERA and 4.38 FIP over 18 starts. Shipped to Atlanta at the trade deadline, he found his mojo. In eight starts he posted a 1.00 ERA and 3.32 FIP. He’s 32 and a constant IL risk, but the upside is there. A team deep in starters could take a look. That wouldn’t be the Royals.

Mize was setting himself up for a big payday. He was having the best season of his career with personal best marks in strikeout rate (8.8 SO/9) and ERA (2.70) with a 2.58 FIP over 16 starts for the Tigers. He really stumbled after a trade to the Padres. He’ll be ok given that he’s a strike-thrower who will be will be 30 next season, he sould be attractive to the Royals as they seek to add depth to their rotation. Doesn't a guy named Casey belong in KC? (Sorry about that!)

Gausman, who will be 36 next year, has been one of the more consistent starting pitchers this decade. While he's lost some velocity and his strikeout rate has declined while his ERA has gone up, the decline phase of his career has been relatively gentle. He's made some noise about retiring but could be tempted with a one-year deal. It wouldn't be a surprise to see him return to Toronto for a final lap. No shade on Gausman, but having him at 20 underscores how thin this free agent class is.

items.title: Royals Off-Season Report
items.author: SRS0=xjif=IU=mg-d0.substack.com=bounce+9ddca1.63af5d-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Although the Royals season mercifully ended a few weeks ago, the 2026 major league season concluded this week with the Milwaukee Brewers winning their first World Series title in franchise history 4 games to 1 over the Tampa Bay Rays.

The crowning of a World Series champion signifies the official start to the MLB off-season. With a lockout of the players looming on Dec. 1, the next few weeks are bound to be jammed full of MLB news. Some of it might even involve the Royals!

  • This means that Alec Marsh’s time in the organization has come to an end. It really looked like he could be in the rotation for some time in 2024, but injuries derailed his career and he hasn’t pitched in over two years now.

    Alex Lange’s time with his hometown team did not go as either had hoped. He finished with a 6.75 ERA and 1.63 WHIP across 60 innings of work. I’m sure he’ll get another shot somewhere.

  • Gonsolin had some decent years with the Dodgers before getting hurt, but this smacks of desperation. Then again, “desperate” might be the best word to describe the Royals starting pitching situation going into 2027.

It’s been fairly quiet on the rumor front, but a few are starting to circulate around the Royals.

  • Look, it’s not going to happen. The Royals aren’t going to trade Bobby Baseball. That said, if I’m Picollo and the Red Sox actually make this offer…I take it.

  • Vinnie, Massey, and of course Bobby were consistently excellent, but Loftin? Really? His defense at third is better than at second, but I’m not sure it is Gold Glove caliber. Winners will be announced Sunday evening on ESPN.

Beginning next Tuesday (11/3), teams can start signing free agents and making trades. Remember that is a process that sometimes lasts the entire three months of a normal off-season. With the impending lockout on Dec. 2nd, teams will have to cram all of their acquisitions into less than a month.

It’s hard for me to fit my brain around the idea of signing some guy to a gazillion dollar contract when you don’t even know the rules the game is going to be played under next season. Will there be a salary cap? A salary floor? Will there even be a season in 2027?

items.title: Welcome to the offseason
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
With the World Series over and the Milwaukee Brewers the rightful champions, it’s time to end my annual postseason sabbatical. After all this time, and as the cliché goes, I hope this edition of the newsletter finds you well.

Even though we’re yet to November, I plan on pacing myself as much as possible to keep the newsletter productive during what is shaping up to be a lengthy lockout once the current CBA expires on December 1. When the owners lockout the players (an unnecessary move at this point in the process), the baseball world will grind to a halt. Sadly, we’ve seen this movie before, so we know the baseball desert that awaits. The Winter Meetings will be cancelled. There will be few or no negotiating sessions though the holidays. The urgency will return when we should have camps opening in February.

It’s going to be a colder winter than usual.

As for what I plan to do here, there will be some player profiles, some random (i.e. wrong) free agent guesses and, of course, I'll cover any news that happens over the next month ahead of the lockout. Along with the usual baseball foolishness. So hit that subscribe button if you haven't so we can make this offseason journey together.

The first order now that the offseason is officially underway is for teams to massage their 40-man roster. There will probably be a flurry of activity ahead of the lockout and for now at least, it's business as usual. The Royals saw Jonathan India, Craig Kimbrel, Luke Maile and Josh Rojas officially become free agents on Thursday. On Monday, this quartet will be free to negotiate with the rest of the teams in the league. I can’t imagine a scenario where any of these guys will be back with the Royals.

Late Thursday, word came down that Carlos Estévez will soon join them on the market as the Royals declined his $13 million club option. They’ll hand over $2 million instead as a buyout. Estévez recorded one out all year and gave up a walkoff grand slam. It wasn't what anyone was looking for.

Tony Gonsolin, who signed a major league contract in August and also appeared in one game for the Royals, had his 2027 option picked up. His outing was in September against the White Sox where he looked good for two innings before the wheels came off in his third frame of work. Still, you could see some of that old magic that made him appealing to the Royals. For next season, the oft-injured pitcher will be officially on the books for $2.5 million, although there are reports he can earn up to $6 million in performance incentives.

Once the Royals move their players off the 60-day IL, the Royals will have 38 players on the 40-man roster.

What did you think of the postseason? Overall I thought it was fine, helped by the fact the Brewers and the Rays won their respective leagues. I also low-key enjoyed the fact that the higher seeded team won every matchup in every round. Underdogs are fun, but seeing good teams advance is satisfying. My only issue: The dominance of the Milwaukee nine removed any semblance of drama from these last couple of weeks. They are such a complete ballclub that this October felt akin to 1984 when the Detroit Tigers steamrolled to victory or 1989 when it was the Oakland A’s getting down to business after coming up short the year before. While nothing is ever certain in these playoffs, especially with the expanded format, but once the Brewers started throwing haymakers at the Dodgers in the NLCS, it all seemed settled.

A couple of stray World Series thoughts as we process a long winter (and probably spring) ahead...

  • I felt the similarities between the Brewers and the 2015 Royals in that both teams played a form of what I’ve taken to call Total Baseball in that they do just about everything right. Strong starting pitching? Check. A selfless move-the-line batting order? Uh-huh. A lockdown bullpen? For sure. Clutch hits, including home runs? Yep. Hell, both teams check the box with salt of the earth managers who are refreshingly honest.

There was a moment in the dying moments of the NLCS where the broadcast was doing the obligatory crowd shots and found a woman who looked like she was about to pass out. It was a combination of stress and disbelief. It was the most relatable thing I saw all October, making me think of when I had to take a seat while in the upper tank at The K for Game Four of the 2014 ALCS. I seemed to have gotten a bit lightheaded. When something is unfolding in front of you that you never, ever thought would happen, it can hit hard. I sure she rallied and partied in an appropriate manner.

As we know, winning a championship after suffering through years of heartache makes the moment all the sweeter.

  • As a self-proclaimed broadcast geek, I have to wonder why American broadcasting networks hate their viewers so much. After a summer spent watching the World Cup on Univision to dodge the audio assault from Fox soccer announcers, I found myself regularly wondering if we really need nine innings (or more) of John Smoltz who was seemingly getting paid by the word? No, we don’t and I found myself often wishing he would just shut up. There are moments where he does bring up an interesting point or two regarding strategy and whatnot, but for the most part in this World Series he was shockingly unprepared. Fox does a huge disservice by having him on the broadcast. Maybe someday TBS will get the rights to the World Series and they can have Brian Anderson, Ron Darling and Jeff Francoeur on the call. Anderson, the Brewers TV guy when not on national assignments is a pro. Darling is part of the best booth in baseball for the Mets. And Frenchy is really, really good at providing commentary to the point that I wish we could’ve enticed him to stay in Kansas City at the end of his career.
  • I’m not surprised the early television ratings for the World Series were, while down, better than expected. While the five games weren’t exactly what I would call crisp baseball, even casual fans can appreciate when the two best teams in the game face off for the championship. It also helps that both teams embraced the moment and seemed to just have fun playing the game.
  • Speaking of the keep-the-line-moving mentality of the Milwaukee lineup, I’m going to be thinking about the fifth inning of Game Three for a long, long time. It was epic baseball, a symphony of exit velocity, launch angle and perfectly placed hits. In an October with close games and seemingly few extended rallies, this inning was unforgettable.
  • I know newspapers are struggling for survival, but I can’t help but continue to be disappointed by the lack of baseball coverage provided by the Kansas City Star. It wasn’t difficult to come up with a local angle with Grain Valley’s Jacob Misiorowski and Park Hill’s Aaron Ashby both playing key rolls for the Brewers. They should’ve sent someone to cover this Series.
  • Remember when we had Andy McCullough writing about the Royals at The Star? He had the World Series wrap for The Athletic. It is, as you would expect, exceptional.

As McCullough points out, the Brewers have not had an easy road even though they’ve qualified for October in eight of the last nine seasons. They’ve made several trades along the way of key players including pitchers Josh Hader, Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta. Not all of those deals yielded players who landed on their postseason roster. They filled the gaps through a strong international presence, outstanding scouting and exceptional drafts. It’s not an easy blueprint to replicate, but when you look at what Milwaukee General Manager Matt Arnold has done on the trade front, you have to wonder about how the Royals have failed to capitalize on peak return on some players they should’ve dealt. Missed opportunities equal missed postseasons.

items.title: Second to none
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
One Wisconsin man, waiting for a flight to Milwaukee, stood and gazed at the sign two gates away: Tampa. Another, splayed on the airport carpet, trying to wrangle his restless kids with an iPad showing the Packers game, said he had just come from there, had tried to rearrange his family’s schedule to stay for two, three more days. Because the Brewers, by then up 2-0 in the World Series, were on their way.

This was in Nashville, Sunday afternoon. My wife and I were sitting at the gate in between, headed back to New York. All weekend, we had marveled at the preponderance of Brewers fans traipsing around town in jerseys, T-shirts, hats, talking about ticket prices and family members who ponied up, who skipped planned vacations to watch the franchise’s first World Series championship.

In a city 564 miles from Milwaukee, everyone with any connection to Wisconsin was making sure to show it. And 725 miles from Tropicana Field, almost halfway there, they were thinking about Tampa, glancing toward it, itching to be there for their heroes’ increasingly imminent, some might say inevitable, coronation.

When the moment arrived Wednesday night — the Brewers taking the game and the series over the Rays, 4-1 — thousands of fans in blue and yellow injected the road ballpark with the rapture of home. Thousands more were at American Family Field to jubilate together. The enthusiasm, the reach, of major-league baseball’s smallest city felt huge.

The Brewers’ title was not sudden, not a surprise. It rode atop a swell of success that has been building since 2016, under David Stearns’ front office and then roaring on through Matt Arnold’s promotion from within. Eight postseason appearances, six division crowns, three NLCS appearances. An MVP, a Cy Young and another in the offing. Pride was there, with plenty of reason for it. But it was closely held, a targeted fire hose rather than a crashing wave, until this week.

The impulse, mine and yours and the masses’, is to explain a newly observed phenomenon, to track that wave back to its origin. Their Triple-A affiliate is in Nashville, could that be … no the tie only dates to 2020. Were the Packers in town facing the Titans? Nope.

Is this America’s team for dethroning the Dodgers? Are the 2026 Brewers the protagonists of a soaring sequel to Moneyball? Are they a blueprint being copied as they are celebrated?

Is this how any team would feel on the cusp of its first championship? Is this what it looks like when the search for an explanation widens beyond logic, beyond words, and opens up into something that can only be described as an experience?

The day it was agreed to back in December 2022, a three-way trade between the Braves, A’s and Brewers was called the Sean Murphy deal. The offshoot of the trade that redirected catcher William Contreras to the Brewers for speedster Esteury Ruiz was a noteworthy but secondary concern.

History has perspective that headlines don’t. Last night, as Contreras hit, challenged and implored his way to World Series MVP honors, the Brewers forced the baseball world to look at them from a new angle. Because of money or media concentration or the happenstance of postseason results, the club with the most wins over the past three seasons has not been held in the regard that record would imply.

Their championship and vengeful sweep of the Dodgers barrels the sport out of a particular type of tunnel vision. For years and years, as the postseason field expanded, “it was easy to see the playoffs as a crapshoot,” Matthew Trueblood wrote recently.

“Then, Shohei Ohtani signed with the Dodgers and won it all twice in a row, and it was like the God particle had been discovered all over again,” Trueblood said. “That messy egalitarianism that seemed to have settled over the sport burned off like low-lying fog on an unseasonably warm autumn morning, and we all saw (or imagined, at least) the ugly truth: Only power matters; only money wins.”

There was a time, not three years ago, when the Dodgers’ long run of excellence was still unvested. They were the best team in baseball, but that was valued on paper rather than in gold.

Overnight, the Brewers have called for a new assessment. The season they just completed — 103 wins, with an 11-2 playoff mission completed against the best competition available — was second to none. In degree of dominance and difficulty, it compares favorably to every champ since the 2018 Red Sox. They are two regular season wins clear of the Dodgers in the very years of the supposed Ohtani dynasty, they have a World Series pennant headed to the rafters, a young team and booming farm system in tow.

Is this Brewers team an underdog story with a happy ending or an adamant arrival of something else entirely?

How, exactly, did you grow up? How did you fall in love? How did you get to where you are today? Do you really know? Was there a discrete, usable process involved? Or do you, in the grand tradition of the major religions, recount a singular story with the conviction of universal truth?

The Brewers’ motto was everywhere in October: . But it’s a mantra, not an invitation. Milwaukee’s way lends itself to uncertainty. Under Stearns and Arnold, they have sustained winning teams on a middling ownership-imposed budgets by trading away a number of established stars (Corbin Burnes, Josh Hader, Devin Williams, Freddy Peralta) in favor of starter packs full of young, promising, unknown commodities. They fill out rosters by sifting for high-potential waiver claims and unheralded trade chips, not winning free agent bidding wars.

In 2026, they wound up with three of the 30 most valuable players in baseball, and those players were 24 (Jacob Misiorowski), 26 (Brice Turang) and 22 (Jackson Chourio). Turang’s breakout last year was the only 4-WAR season among the group entering the spring. Two more 3-WAR hitters (Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell) had never even amassed 500 plate appearances in a single major-league season. The starting shortstop who batted .354 in the postseason (Cooper Pratt) had not yet glimpsed Triple-A.

They gave rookie pitchers 80 starts, more than any other team in the sport. The oldest and least acclaimed of those arms, Robert Gasser, finished with the most starts and registered the best starting pitching performance of the World Series.

Uncertainty, in such regular doses, is hard to distinguish from skepticism when viewed through a quantified lens.

Over this decade-long ascent, the Brewers have persistently outfoxed wise and grounded projection systems. First, they did it under the professorial watch of Stearns and Craig Counsell. When Counsell took a larger contract for the rival Cubs, Arnold promoted Pat Murphy, grizzled motivator of men, the most football coach of baseball manager. He delights in the undershot projections, feeding them to his team like fuel to a fire.

So many of them had felt like they were second-best, the second choice. And the ones who hadn’t? Well, Murphy made sure they would, as part of the collective unit that was less proven than the Dodgers, less appealing than the Cubs, less respected than they had earned.

Projecting the Brewers to do all the things they did would have been malpractice. Not projecting all those things turned out to be wrong. Would you believe it if you didn’t see it?

Belief is necessary. It’s the quotidian forward force, the gas in the combustion engine that carries you to work and the grocery store and back home again. Seeing, with thousands of others who waited and believed alongside you on the same warm nights, sitting in the same traffic, that’s transcendent. It’s the wind in your hair at sunset, driving 75 on a wide open highway. It's the thing you get up and start each day to reach.

Throngs of Brewers fans took over Tropicana Field to see something bigger and less nebulous than overachievement. Like the outfield fences, the walls of collective understanding are arbitrarily drawn. Winning the World Series isn’t necessarily harder than winning 103 games or winning the division every year, but getting over that wall means something different. It’s a license for collective joy.

It gets Christian Yelich jerseys packed in suitcases and Chourio jerseys purchased a size bigger than the kids need right now. It gets plane tickets booked and tattoos designed. It moves broadcasters and Cy Young winners to tears.

No explanation is needed. ⚾️

Jacob Misiorowski has found a perfect match. The woman who gave the broadcast a fantastic GIF-able facial expression …

In addition to being the most football coach of baseball managers, Pat Murphy is the obvious choice for a hypothetical Reporters’ Favorite award.

He even threw in an intentional mispronunciation of social media quip, which has a 100% chance of being quoted. “I’m not on social media, Twizzler or Instacart, whatever,” the AP has Murphy saying.

I’m not accusing anyone of bias. I’m just noting the reality that Murphy is both constitutionally and topically perfect for the baseball media.

Contreras’ older brother Willson, who has been openly affected by the hardship in their native country, was on hand wearing his brother’s jersey and tearfully celebrating with him on the field afterward.

Joe Davis, the lead FOX play-by-play announcer, specializes in echos of baseball broadcasts past.

When the Rays eventually came back to win in 12, he joined the linage of his predecessor, Joe Buck (who was adapting his own father’s call), when he yelled, “We’ll see you later tonight,” over the post-midnight walk-off knock.

Davis’ flair for the cleverly deployed reference sometimes overshadows his original work, which tends toward the strong but subtle. But this is another area where time will crystallize the potency of the work. Last year, he punctuated the Dodgers’ epic Game 7 win with one I could see sticking for the ages: “To beat the champ, you gotta knock ‘em out.”

“Unshakeable, unstoppable, and champions at last: The Milwaukee Brewers.”

The part where I ask for your support

This is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.

I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

items.title: The Limbo Plays
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
It started to feel familiar in the 11th inning. A first baseman drew a walk. A pinch-runner took his place, then stole second. The Rays, down 3-0 and staring down the end, got a whiff of what could be.

World Series Game 4 chanted the words itself, really. Broadcaster Joe Davis just identified the apparition that was summoned: Dave Roberts, the 2004 Red Sox, David Ortiz, the only comeback from down 3-0 in baseball history. This runner — Jorge Mateo, in for Yandy Diaz — didn’t end up scoring. But like the first chapter of that Red Sox comeback, this game ended in a 12th-inning walk-off that preserved the seeds of Rays hope and Brewers doubt.

The Game 4 moments that were and weren’t to be are suspended in a reality between Good and Bad, History and Forgotten, Something and Nothing.

The vast majority end up in the bin of Nothing, tossed out with the loser’s championship T-shirts. As detailed by Sarah Langs, the Rays are just the 11th team out of 44 in MLB postseason history to even force a Game 5 after going down 3-0. Only four of those came in the World Series, and none have successfully extended it to a Game 6. The 2024 Yankees avoided a sweep, with Anthony Volpe hitting a pivotal homer in Game 4, only to succumb to the Dodgers in Game 5. Prior to that, the last World Series team down 3-0 to even win Game 4 was in 1970.

For now, the tension is in our blindness. We don’t if the plays that riveted us late last night and early this morning are Big Papis or little Volpes. Rays fans have to hold onto them, hoping they last. Brewers fans have to live with them, willing them to go away.

While they mean the most and the least to us, let’s rank the plays from World Series Game 4 that could turn the most pungent with time.

8. Rays let a Jake Bauers foul pop-up drop, but strike him out — top of the 10th inning

It feels like the Brewers have been feasting off their opponents’ mistakes, growing more powerful with each slip-up. When Liam Hicks and Junior Caminero stumbled into a classic blooper reel drop, it gave the Brewers an extra opportunity with a full count and two outs in the 10th. Imminent doom, a Bauers homer, felt like the only outcome that could follow. But it didn’t.

This was one of four times after reaching the 2-2 deadlock that the Brewers left a man on base, and one of two times Bauers made the third out.

7. Chandler Simpson catches Garrett Mitchell’s fly ball at the wall — top 9th

Simpson’s grab was visually pleasing, but ultimately was never really precarious for the Rays despite the elevated tenor of the broadcast. Still, if Simpson’s outfield chops had been at his dreadful 2025 levels, the runner taking off from first might very well have scored.

6. Junior Caminero dodges David Hamilton’s tag, scores on his errant throw — bottom 4th

The earliest entrant into limbo gave the Rays a 2-1 lead. Jonny DeLuca’s grounder and Caminero’s, uh, unconventional baserunning decision put Brewers third baseman David Hamilton in bind set to fast forward. Surprised to have the opportunity for a tag play, he went after Caminero but missed, then botched the throw to first in his haste to secure an out.

Hamilton rectified the score with a homer the following inning, limiting the mistake’s memory potential.

5. Jonny DeLuca singles in the tying run off Shane Drohan — bottom 12th

Up in the count 1-2 against the least imposing hitter he had faced thus far, Brewers rookie pitcher Shane Drohan needed this. He made an OK pitch — cutter, 90 mph, bending to the outside corner. It just wasn’t sharp enough. DeLuca poked at it and made solid contact up the middle, at which point the game was tied, there were still no outs and the un-double-uppable Simpson coming to the plate. Drohan’s surprise cameo felt cooked.

4. Brewers manager Pat Murphy pulls Aaron Ashby — bottom 11th

Drohan, a rookie lefty who had pitched once in the past month before entering a World Series-clinching save situation, didn’t have it. Probably was never primed to have it in that moment.

The Brewers got to Drohan by being aggressive earlier in the game. Murphy went to closer Trevor Megill in the eighth inning to neutralize the threat of Yandy Diaz, a right-hander, with two outs and no one on base. After just that one out, he turned to Ashby to start the ninth inning against left-handed hitter Jonathan Aranda, relying on the flamethrowing lefty’s ability to stretch multiple innings if needed.

Ashby did, carving through 2 1/3 perfect innings. But eventually Murphy reached the limit of his comfort zone with a pitcher he wants available for whatever may come next.

“The velo was down quite a bit,” Murphy told reporters afterward. “We can tell when Ashby’s ball doesn’t have the same movement and the same finish. So it was time.”

Having burned through his usual leverage options, Murphy went to Antonio Senzatela, then summoned Drohan after Senzatela had faced four batters, getting two outs and falling victim to a play still to come on the list.

I don’t know if Ashby was good for five more outs. And Murphy couldn’t have known that Cooper Pratt was about to smash the biggest homer of his life, that a potential finish line was approaching. The options remaining were such, and Ashby’s October dominance is at such historic levels, that the decision will raise an eyebrow or two for as long as it lives on.

3. Ben Williamson chops a walk-off single over first base — bottom 12th

Called off the bench, the last bat available to Rays manager Kevin Cash had to make contact, at the bare minimum. And he did.

2. Cooper Pratt caught stealing by a whisker — top 9th

Andrew Vaughn is this game’s man who wasn’t there. A dangerous hitter relegated to bench duty by Bauers’s breakout, Vaughn was pinch-hitting when Pratt took off for second.

The throw and tag were a sort of combination miracle, with catcher Liam Hicks’ ball tailing just into the path of Pratt’s sliding glove, trailing behind his body. He was safe but for the cosmic grace of a baseball god that wanted more baseball.

Yet the same speed that allowed for the steal might have allowed Pratt to score without it. Vaughn is a strong contact hitter. Even though his power is superior against lefty pitchers — he was facing right-handed Rays closer Bryan Baker — Vaughn struck out only 17.7% of the time against righties this year and batted .285. He also reached base at a .369 clip against right-handers. The chances of a ball in play, or a free pass to second, were pretty good.

Wasting Vaughn’s appearance, which ended immediately without an official at-bat, was a missed opportunity.

1. Caminero reaches on a bounced throw from Joey Ortiz that Bauers can’t pick — bottom 12th

Errors are like a toothache. You can’t resist prodding, checking if it still hurts. Yep, it does.

This one was charged to Ortiz, a superlative defender who fielded a bounding grounder cautiously against the lumbering Caminero, then threw a one-hopper that Bauers couldn’t handle at first. It ended Senzatela’s outing, put a runner on and set off the spiral that took the Brewers from championship clinch to sphincter clenched.

"There's no excuse," Ortiz said postgame. "Not one at all. I should make that play every (bleeping) time.”

You could easily debit the mistake to Bauers, mentally. It might be an in-between hop, but it was a one-hop throw on line, with the runner nowhere near the bag. It was the sort of split-second mistake the Brewers usually churn into runs. It’s the sort of split-second mistake that can last forever, or fade into nothing by Friday. Until then, it’s a raw nerve. ⚾️

The part where I ask for your support

This is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.

I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Leading from below
items.author: bounces+qdumm2z8xes7hvg4dzxblh889o44lf4hl36q@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about leading from below. This may be the most difficult kind of leadership—leading when you're not the one in charge. The key is to identify when it's appropriate to be a good team member, helping move things forward, and when it's right to raise your hand and offer suggestions to leadership.

This may be the most difficult type of leadership.

There will be situations where you are a team on paper but, for whatever reason, you have insight or experience that is equal to or even exceeds that of your team’s leaders.

In situations like this, you may find that you frequently disagree with leadership’s direction, decisions, tactics, or other aspects of the team’s work. You may feel a strong urge to express those opinions, but you’ll mostly want to resist that urge.

Reserve the times to talk with the leadership team for when you are substantially opposed to their plan because you’re concerned it will cause significant issues down the road. And when you share that sort of feedback with them, be sure to privately correct, publicly praise; that principle applies here as much as anywhere else.

The best way you can lead from below is to try to lead in situations where you are concerned about a bad outcome. If you are constantly offering input, nitpicking, and otherwise trying to insert yourself into the leadership process, you will eventually be ignored.​

“The Boy Who Cried Wolf” is a cautionary tale here. You don’t want to offer input so frequently that you are ignored the one time it

counts.

Build up your credibility and use it only when it really matters.
